A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical spectrum of the remnant is more complex and less hot than previously thought.
the remnant has an age of about 500 years, and is in an evolutionary stage where the shock is still interacting with a dense medium, and where the pulsar wind nebula is not yet fully developed.

the optical spectrum of the SNR 054-69.3 is consistent with the previous results, and the spectrum of the pulsar has a steeper energy distribution than previously thought, with no significant contribution from a non-thermal component.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the optical emission of the pulsar in 0540- 69.3 has a steeper spectral slope than previously thought, and that this may be related to the fact that the pulsar has an unusually high surface magnetic field of ∼4 × 10 ^{12}  G.
the optical emission from the pulsar is not a simple thermal blackbody, as was previously assumed, but rather a combination of thermal and non-thermal radiation.
the pulsar nebular emission is a major contaminant in optical spectroscopic studies, and must be accounted for when interpreting the results.
